paragraphs: Deep topic models aim to represent documents at several levels of abstraction, starting from counts of the words they contain. Their higher layers can suffer from posterior collapse: instead of capturing useful distinctions, the latent representations become repetitive or uninformative. This paper addresses the resulting loss of representational capacity.

The first contribution changes how documents are generated from the model’s hidden representations. The authors add skip connections that create stronger links between the document and multiple latent layers. This gives the higher layers a more direct connection to the information that the model must explain.

The second contribution combines data augmentation with a reformulation of that generative process as a Markov decision process. This allows the authors to develop a policy-gradient training algorithm intended to further reduce information loss at higher layers. Experiments show that these changes alleviate posterior collapse and produce higher-quality document representations. The stated result is an improvement in the usefulness of the hierarchy, rather than a claim that collapse is eliminated.
neurips-2022-alleviating-posterior-colla.tldr: Skip connections and policy-gradient training help deep topic models retain useful information in their higher latent layers.

paragraphs: Video-language models can forget previously learned relationships when training continues on new data. The paper studies this problem through a continual learning setting in which a model encounters five video-text datasets sequentially, each with a different distribution. Methods that retain past training examples or expand the network can become resource intensive in this setting.

BMU-MoCo modifies a cross-modal momentum-encoder model so that information moves in both directions during training. Momentum updates affect both the momentum encoders and the main encoders at every step. This lets the main model revisit knowledge retained in the momentum encoders while learning from the current dataset.

The method also maintains a pair of global momentum encoders initialized only at the start, using the same bidirectional update strategy to draw on earlier knowledge. Experiments report better video-text retrieval and less forgetting than recent competitors, without extra data or dynamically growing networks. The contribution is a mechanism for retaining useful knowledge within the model’s update process while continuing to adapt to changing video-text data.
neurips-2022-bmu-moco-bidirectional-mome.tldr: BMU-MoCo uses bidirectional momentum updates to improve continual video-text learning without extra data or growing networks.

paragraphs: The maximum clique problem asks for the largest group of graph nodes in which every pair is connected. Finding an exact solution is NP-hard, so this paper develops a neural approach for approximating solutions. The model assigns each node a probability of belonging to the maximum clique, then uses a rule-based decoder to produce its final prediction.

Training uses a two-part loss. One part encourages the selection of highly connected nodes, while the other approximates the requirement that the selected nodes form a clique. The architecture incorporates a geometric scattering transform to alleviate oversmoothing, a problem in graph neural networks that would otherwise degrade this approach’s performance.

Empirical results show better solution accuracy and inference speed than representative graph neural network baselines, alongside better results than conventional solvers such as Gurobi under limited time budgets. The model also uses roughly 0.1% as many parameters as previous neural baselines. These findings support an efficient approximation approach; the comparison with conventional solvers specifically concerns restricted computation time.
neurips-2022-can-hybrid-geometric-scatte.tldr: A compact geometric scattering network approximates maximum cliques with strong empirical accuracy and speed under the tested conditions.

paragraphs: In collaborative bandit learning, multiple agents share information through a central server while deciding which actions to try. Sharing can reduce the reward lost while learning, known as regret. But if a fraction of the agents can behave arbitrarily, the same communication can introduce misleading evidence. This paper quantifies that tension for linear stochastic bandits.

The authors construct robust confidence intervals and use them in a phased elimination algorithm. Its regret bound for each trustworthy agent scales, up to logarithmic factors, as the adversarial fraction plus the inverse square root of the number of agents, multiplied by the square root of model dimension times time horizon. When the adversarial fraction is small, the bound demonstrates a benefit from collaboration.

An information-theoretic lower bound matches the result up to the stated qualifications, establishing near-optimal guarantees. The authors also extend their ideas using robust statistics to generalized linear bandits and contextual bandits with changing feature vectors. The results explain both the learning gains available through cooperation and the cost imposed by adversarial participants.
neurips-2022-collaborative-linear-bandit.tldr: Robust collaborative bandit algorithms achieve near-optimal regret bounds that quantify when cooperation remains beneficial despite adversarial agents.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately linear predictors can learn with convex losses while satisfying differential privacy. Its main quantity is excess population risk: the gap between the learned predictor’s expected loss and the best achievable expected loss. The analysis separates two classes of losses because their mathematical properties lead to different privacy costs.

For smooth, nonnegative losses that need not be Lipschitz, including squared loss, the authors establish an upper bound and a corresponding lower bound. Apart from their dependence on the size of the optimal predictor, the bounds are essentially tight in all parameters. This identifies how sample count, dimension, and privacy strength constrain achievable accuracy in that setting.

For Lipschitz losses, the paper closes a previous gap and obtains an optimal rate up to logarithmic factors, with dependence on the design matrix’s rank. This improves existing results in the high-privacy regime. A private model-selection procedure also lets the algorithms achieve their stated rates without knowing the optimal predictor’s size beforehand, removing that advance-information requirement.
neurips-2022-differentially-private-gene.tldr: The paper sharpens privacy–accuracy guarantees for convex linear prediction and achieves them without prior knowledge of the optimal predictor’s size.

paragraphs: Personalized PageRank supports graph tasks including ranking nodes, assigning labels, and constructing embeddings. However, its output can change substantially when just one edge changes. This sensitivity creates a privacy problem: a released representation may reveal information about a relationship in the graph. Existing PageRank algorithms were not designed to control that exposure.

The paper introduces an approximate Personalized PageRank algorithm with a provable bound on its sensitivity to input edges. Controlling this sensitivity supplies a foundation for differentially private graph tools. The authors derive private versions of PageRank ranking, node classification, and node embedding from the same underlying construction.

The accuracy guarantee has a stated condition: when the input graph has large degrees, the approximation achieves accuracy similar to non-private algorithms. The authors also evaluate practical performance empirically. The contribution therefore connects an edge-sensitivity guarantee to several downstream learning operations, while showing that the privacy-oriented approximation can retain useful accuracy in the graph setting covered by the theorem.
neurips-2022-differentially-private-grap.tldr: A sensitivity-bounded approximation to Personalized PageRank enables private graph learning with comparable accuracy on graphs satisfying a large-degree condition.

paragraphs: A deployed classifier may face different class proportions and a class that was absent during training. This paper formalizes that situation as Open Set Label Shift. Its central assumption is that feature distributions within classes remain invariant across domains, even though class frequencies can change arbitrarily and a new class may appear.

The learner must estimate the target class distribution, including the novel class, and build a classifier for that target domain. The authors establish necessary and sufficient conditions for identifying these quantities. They then develop practical methods that use black-box predictors, connecting the problem to label-shift adaptation and positive-unlabeled learning.

Across semi-synthetic benchmarks using vision, language, and medical datasets, the methods consistently outperform the tested open-set adaptation baselines, with reported target-accuracy improvements of 10–25%. The paper also establishes finite-sample convergence for estimating class proportions and convergence to an optimal classifier for linear models in a Gaussian setting. The contribution combines a precisely constrained adaptation problem with algorithms and guarantees tailored to those constraints.
neurips-2022-domain-adaptation-under-ope.tldr: Open Set Label Shift provides methods and conditional guarantees for adapting to changing class proportions and a previously unseen class.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy can perform well under ordinary observations yet be vulnerable when an adversary perturbs those observations. Robust training must account for how these disturbances affect rewards across a sequence of decisions. The paper identifies drawbacks in methods that assess correlated steps separately or jointly train a policy and a separate reinforcement learning attacker.

WocaR-RL directly estimates and optimizes a policy’s worst-case reward under attacks constrained by an l_p perturbation budget. This puts the long-term reward under bounded disturbances at the center of training. It also avoids requiring extra samples to learn an attacker, addressing a source of computational and sampling overhead.

Experiments across multiple environments report state-of-the-art performance against various strong attacks and substantially better training efficiency than prior leading robust training methods. These findings support the practical value of optimizing estimated worst-case reward directly. The attack model remains explicitly bounded, and the reported experimental robustness concerns the strong attacks evaluated in those environments.
neurips-2022-efficient-adversarial-train.tldr: WocaR-RL improves robustness and training efficiency by optimizing estimated worst-case reward without learning a separate attacker.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits choose actions using information available at each decision, balancing promising actions against uncertain ones. Expected improvement is a familiar way to balance exploration and exploitation in Bayesian optimization, but its existing form does not apply directly to contextual bandits. This paper develops that connection through two new algorithms.

For linear reward functions, the authors prove a near-optimal regret guarantee, where regret measures reward lost relative to better decisions. The bound improves on LinTS by a factor equal to the square root of the feature dimension. The algorithm also avoids the per-iteration NP-hard optimization problem identified for LinUCB in the abstract.

The second algorithm models more general reward functions with deep neural networks. Its regret bound scales, up to logarithmic factors, with the effective dimension of a neural tangent kernel matrix times the square root of the number of iterations. Benchmark experiments show that both algorithms consistently outperform the compared approaches, especially in high dimensions. The results give expected improvement both theoretical support and empirical relevance in this broader decision-making setting.
neurips-2022-expected-improvement-for-co.tldr: Two expected-improvement algorithms extend the approach to contextual bandits, with regret guarantees and strong empirical performance in high dimensions.

paragraphs: Transparent glass can be hard to detect because its visual evidence is indirect. Methods that rely on boundaries or reflections may struggle when those cues are absent. This paper instead draws on relationships among objects in a scene: walls and curtains, for example, provide useful context for locating glass windows.

GlassSemNet incorporates this context through two modules. Scene Aware Activation adaptively selects important feature channels using spatial and semantic information. Context Correlation Attention progressively learns relationships among objects, considering both their positions and their meanings. Together, these components let the detector use surrounding scene structure as evidence for glass surfaces.

The authors also introduce GSD-S, a dataset containing 4,519 real-world RGB images with annotations for both glass detection and semantic segmentation. Experiments show that GlassSemNet outperforms contemporary methods, including a reported 42.6% improvement in mean absolute error on GSD-S. The findings support semantic context as a useful source of information for a detection task where the target itself can provide weak visual cues.
neurips-2022-exploiting-semantic-relatio.tldr: GlassSemNet uses spatial and semantic relationships among scene objects to improve glass detection, supported by a new annotated dataset.

paragraphs: Face animation needs to reproduce motion while retaining a person’s identity and detailed appearance. Complex facial deformation makes these goals difficult to achieve together. FNeVR addresses the problem by combining two-dimensional motion warping and three-dimensional volume rendering within one network, bringing both forms of image modeling into the animation process.

Its Face Volume Rendering module is designed to improve facial details in the rendered image. The network first extracts three-dimensional information and then uses an orthogonal adaptive ray-sampling module for efficient rendering. The approach therefore incorporates a three-dimensional rendering stage alongside the two-dimensional handling of motion.

FNeVR also includes a lightweight pose editor, allowing the facial pose to be adjusted through the framework. Extensive experiments on widely used talking-head benchmarks report the best overall quality and performance among the evaluated approaches. These findings support the combined framework as a way to improve face animation, with its rendering module addressing detail and its pose editor providing an additional form of control.
neurips-2022-fnevr-neural-volume-renderi.tldr: FNeVR combines 2D motion warping, 3D volume rendering, and lightweight pose editing to improve talking-head animation.

paragraphs: A pretrained generator learns a broad output distribution, while an application may need a particular subset or a more balanced mix of attributes. PromptGen addresses this mismatch by using knowledge from other available models to control what an existing generator samples. Its focus is the distribution of generated outputs, including combinations of desired characteristics.

The framework represents the desired control with an energy-based model. It then approximates that model using invertible neural networks, enabling feed-forward image sampling without optimization at inference time. This makes the learned control usable through a direct sampling process.

Experiments demonstrate several forms of control across multiple unconditional generators. CLIP supplies text guidance, classifiers support balancing attributes or attribute combinations, and inverse graphics models support generating the same identity in different poses. The authors also identify reporting bias when CLIP provides the control signal and show that PromptGen can iteratively reduce bias in the resulting distribution. The findings illustrate both the flexibility of borrowing control signals from existing models and the need to account for biases those signals introduce.
neurips-2022-generative-visual-prompt-un.tldr: PromptGen learns efficient sampling controls for pretrained generators using existing models for text guidance, attribute balancing, and pose control.

paragraphs: Graph edit distance and subgraph edit distance are expressive ways to compare graphs, but computing either exactly is NP-hard. Neural approximations can reduce computation, yet prediction accuracy alone is insufficient. Some downstream operations require mathematical distance properties, and subgraph edit distance introduces the additional complication of being asymmetric.

GREED uses a siamese graph neural network with an inductive bias designed to preserve the relevant properties while learning these distances. This addresses both metric requirements for graph edit distance and the asymmetry of subgraph comparison. Preserving the triangle inequality also makes the learned embeddings suitable for indexing, connecting the model’s structure to faster search.

Experiments cover ten real graph datasets containing up to seven million edges. GREED is reported to be more accurate than the compared state of the art and up to three orders of magnitude faster. With indexing, CPU-only computations are up to fifty times faster than the closest baseline’s GPU computations. These are reported experimental advantages, showing how property preservation can improve practical search as well as distance prediction.
neurips-2022-greed-a-neural-framework-fo.tldr: GREED learns property-preserving graph distances whose indexable embeddings enable accurate and fast graph similarity search.

paragraphs: Human visual learning combines rapid adaptation with knowledge accumulation over much longer periods. This paper introduces two benchmarks to examine those abilities in self-supervised learning algorithms. One measures whether models match human behavioral changes over minutes and hours; the other uses a purely online learning sequence derived from children’s visual experience across years of development.

None of the evaluated algorithms perfectly matches human performance. BYOL, SwAV, and MAE perform substantially worse on these benchmarks than earlier approaches such as SimCLR and MoCo-v2. The authors’ analysis indicates that difficulty handling sparse, low-diversity data streams is the primary reason for the newer methods’ failures. Using memory through negative sampling appears helpful in those environments.

The benchmarks also reveal a tension between responsiveness and retention. An algorithm needs enough sensitivity to local context to reproduce rapid learning changes, while remaining stable enough to avoid forgetting over longer periods. The contribution provides a quantitative comparison with human learning and evidence that mechanisms for memory and sample comparison strongly affect performance under these naturalistic learning conditions.
neurips-2022-how-well-do-unsupervised-le.tldr: Two human-learning benchmarks reveal weaknesses in self-supervised algorithms on sparse visual streams and a trade-off between rapid adaptation and long-term retention.

paragraphs: Sensory neuroprostheses aim to restore or augment perception, but the sensations produced by current devices can be distorted. Predicting the response to an electrical stimulus is only part of the problem. A useful encoding strategy must work in the opposite direction: given a desired response, determine which stimulus should produce it.

The Hybrid Neural Autoencoder frames this inverse problem as end-to-end optimization. A deep neural network learns to encode the desired input into stimulation, while a known, fixed forward model approximates how the biological system responds. Training the encoder through this model ties stimulus selection to the response it is intended to create.

As a proof of concept in visual neuroprostheses, the method produces high-fidelity, patient-specific stimuli for handwritten digits and segmented images of everyday objects. It significantly outperforms conventional encoding strategies across all simulated patients. These results support the approach within the simulated evaluation and suggest a possible route toward other neuroprosthetic applications; the demonstrated finding concerns model-based stimulus encoding rather than restored vision in patients.
neurips-2022-hybrid-neural-autoencoders-.tldr: A neural stimulus encoder trained through a fixed biological-response model improves simulated visual neuroprosthesis encoding.

paragraphs: Image animation transfers motion from a driving video to the appearance supplied by source images. This paper develops a framework that can use a set of source images, allowing the animation process to draw on different available features. The challenge is to determine which source information corresponds to the current driving image and how to place it.

The proposed method handles these operations with a single cross-modal attention layer. It finds correspondences, selects suitable features from different source images, and warps those selected features. Feature selection and motion transfer are therefore combined within the same implicit warping mechanism.

The authors contrast this with explicit flow-based warping, which was designed around a single source and does not extend well to multiple sources. Their framework’s ability to choose among source features helps it achieve state-of-the-art results across multiple animation datasets, using either one source image or several. The stated findings show that a mechanism built to exploit image sets can also perform strongly in the single-source setting.
neurips-2022-implicit-warping-for-animat.tldr: A single attention layer selects and warps features from source image sets to animate them using motion from a driving video.

paragraphs: Zero-shot classification often recognizes unseen categories through attributes that connect them to known categories. However, obtaining the attribute annotations used during training can itself be expensive. This paper asks whether zero-shot learning can instead produce detectors for unseen attributes, allowing those detectors to help annotate data automatically.

Zero-Shot Learning for Attributes starts with a small set of detectors trained on manually labeled attributes. It applies set operations to decompose those seen attributes into basic components, then recombines the components to synthesize detectors for novel attributes. The approach uses structure within known attributes to build new detection capabilities.

Experiments show that the synthesized detectors capture novel attribute semantics and outperform the compared baselines in detection and localization. The authors also use them to re-annotate the Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 dataset. Several generalized zero-shot classification algorithms trained with these automatic annotations achieve performance comparable to training with manual ground-truth annotations. This supports the proposed detectors as a way to reduce annotation effort in the demonstrated application.
neurips-2022-make-an-omelette-with-break.tldr: ZSLA synthesizes unseen attribute detectors by decomposing and recombining known attributes, supporting automatic dataset annotation.

paragraphs: Hierarchical and ontological multi-label classification assigns multiple labels to an item while accounting for relationships among labels in a graph. This paper argues that existing benchmarks cover too little of that problem space to support broad conclusions. It examines three dimensions: available features, the distribution of labels across examples, and graph structure.

The analysis identifies several sources of confounding. Missing rich features can prevent modern representation learning from serving as an appropriate baseline. In most common benchmarks, over 40% of labels have fewer than five training examples, mixing classification performance with few-shot learning difficulty. Correlations between performance and tree height also help explain variation in results.

Ontologue is a declarative query system for creating benchmarks with specified properties. The authors use it to construct four new benchmarks from DBPedia and evaluate leading algorithms on both existing and new datasets. Performance conclusions vary substantially across the examined dimensions. The system therefore provides a way to investigate which problem characteristics support a result and how broadly that result may generalize.
neurips-2022-ontologue-declarative-bench.tldr: Ontologue generates customizable graph-structured classification benchmarks to reveal how dataset properties change performance conclusions.

paragraphs: Matching near-infrared face images with visible-light images is difficult because the two modalities differ substantially and paired training data are scarce. This paper addresses both issues by generating paired facial images and designing a learning objective that emphasizes identity across the two image types.

The generation process reconstructs three-dimensional face shape and reflectance from a large two-dimensional face dataset. A new transformation converts visible-light reflectance to near-infrared reflectance. A physically based renderer then produces high-resolution images across different identities and poses in both spectra. The proposed identity-based maximum mean discrepancy loss reduces the modality gap and encourages attention to identity rather than details such as pose or accessories.

Experiments on four NIR-VIS recognition benchmarks show performance comparable to leading methods without requiring existing NIR-VIS recognition datasets. With slight fine-tuning on the target datasets, the method significantly exceeds the reported state of the art. The findings support synthetic paired data and identity-focused learning as a combined response to limited cross-modality training data.
neurips-2022-physically-based-face-rende.tldr: Physically rendered paired faces and an identity-focused loss improve matching between near-infrared and visible-light face images.

paragraphs: AdderNet replaces costly convolution multiplications with addition-based L1 computations to improve energy efficiency. Using low-bit representations could further improve hardware efficiency, but standard convolutional quantization methods do not transfer directly. Existing AdderNet approaches use one shared scale for weights and activations, which can cause substantial accuracy loss at low precision.

The paper analyzes differences between weight and activation distributions and introduces a redistribution-based quantization method. It clusters pretrained full-precision kernels into groups, sharing a scale within each group while allowing separate scales across groups. It also adds a lossless range clamp for weights and an outlier-clamping strategy for activations to compensate for distribution differences.

Experiments on several benchmarks support the method’s effectiveness. A four-bit post-training quantized adder ResNet-18 reaches 66.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet, reported as about 8.5% higher than previous AdderNet quantization methods at comparable energy efficiency. The result shows that adapting scales and ranges to AdderNet’s particular computation can materially improve low-bit accuracy.
neurips-2022-redistribution-of-weights-a.tldr: Grouped scales and tailored range clamping improve low-bit AdderNet accuracy while retaining comparable energy efficiency.

paragraphs: Probabilistic inference often requires samples from a target distribution known only in unnormalized form. Stein Variational Gradient Descent approaches this by repeatedly moving a collection of particles to approximate the target. Its asymptotic connection to single-objective optimization motivates this paper’s question: can a related sampling method address multiple objectives through multiple target distributions?

Stochastic Multiple Target Sampling Gradient Descent extends the construction to several unnormalized targets. It moves through intermediate distributions that gradually orient toward those targets, guiding particles into regions where the targets jointly assign high likelihood. This gives the method a way to account for several probabilistic objectives within one evolving particle collection.

The authors show that, in their asymptotic analysis, the method reduces exactly to the multiple-gradient descent algorithm used in multi-objective optimization. This supplies the intended theoretical connection between sampling and optimization with several objectives. Experiments demonstrate the approach’s merits for multi-task learning, supporting its use where the learning process needs to accommodate multiple target distributions together.
neurips-2022-stochastic-multiple-target-.tldr: MT-SGD guides particles toward jointly high-likelihood regions of multiple targets and connects asymptotically to multi-objective gradient descent.

paragraphs: Sequential event prediction estimates what happens next from a history of events. Models trained on sequences collected at one time may later encounter different distributions. This paper studies that temporal shift through a data-generating perspective, focusing on hidden context that influences both the historical sequence and the next event.

The authors establish a negative result for existing maximum-likelihood approaches under distribution shift caused by this latent confounder. They then construct a learning objective based on backdoor adjustment, a way of accounting for common causes in causal analysis. Variational inference makes the resulting objective tractable for sequence learning.

The proposed framework also uses hierarchical branching structures to learn representations specific to different contexts. Experiments across diverse tasks, including sequential recommendation, demonstrate effectiveness, applicability, and scalability with several existing models as backbones. The contribution connects a particular explanation for temporal prediction failure to a corresponding training objective and representation structure, with empirical evidence that the framework can improve learning across the tested applications.
neurips-2022-towards-out-of-distribution.tldr: A causal learning objective and context-specific representations address temporal shifts driven by hidden common causes in event sequences.

paragraphs: Neural decoding translates neural activity into quantities such as intended movement velocity. The relationship between activity and intention can change over time, making a fixed decoder unreliable. EvoEnsemble addresses this problem by adapting the decoder as the incoming signal changes, treating the changing functional relationship as something to track online.

The framework combines evolutionary computation with Bayesian modeling. At each time slot, incoming data provide likelihoods used to assess the fitness of candidate models. This supplies an ongoing basis for evolving the decoder ensemble in response to the current mapping between neural signals and intended outputs.

Two additional strategies, evolve-at-changes and history-model-archive, are designed to improve efficiency and stability. Experiments using both simulations and neural signals show that EvoEnsemble can track functional changes effectively, improving decoding accuracy and robustness. The largest improvements occur in neural signals with functional changes, aligning the empirical benefit with the problem the framework was designed to solve. The work therefore supports adaptive model evolution as a response to changing neural decoding relationships.
neurips-2022-tracking-functional-changes.tldr: EvoEnsemble evolves a Bayesian ensemble online to track changing neural-signal relationships and improve decoding robustness.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks commonly represent uncertainty through distributions over network parameters. However, expressing useful prior knowledge about the process generating the data can be difficult in parameter space. This paper instead focuses on the distribution over functions represented by the network, which more directly describes its possible predictive behaviors.

The authors formulate Bayesian neural-network inference as estimating a posterior distribution over functions. They propose a scalable variational inference method in this function space, allowing prior information to enter the model while producing predictive uncertainty estimates. This changes the object around which inference is organized, connecting uncertainty modeling to the functions used for prediction.

Across a range of prediction tasks, the method achieves state-of-the-art uncertainty estimation and predictive performance. It also performs well on a challenging medical diagnosis task where reliable uncertainty is important. The findings support function-space inference as a practical way to combine prior information, prediction, and uncertainty estimation, with demonstrated relevance to a safety-critical application.
neurips-2022-tractable-function-space-va.tldr: Scalable function-space variational inference helps Bayesian neural networks incorporate prior knowledge and produce strong predictive uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: Sparse optimization restricts how many components of a solution can be nonzero. Hard-thresholding gradient descent enforces this restriction, but its gradient information may be unavailable or expensive in black-box problems. This paper investigates whether estimates obtained from function evaluations can work reliably with the hard-thresholding step in stochastic optimization.

The proposed SZOHT algorithm combines stochastic zeroth-order gradient estimation with hard thresholding. Its estimator uses a new random support-sampling mechanism. Under standard assumptions, the authors provide a convergence analysis and identify a central tension: errors in the gradient estimate interact with the thresholding operator’s tendency to expand differences.

That analysis yields a theoretical minimum number of random directions for the gradient estimates. It also shows that query complexity is independent of dimension or only weakly dependent on it, depending on the setting. Applications to portfolio optimization and black-box adversarial attacks illustrate the method’s utility. The contribution explains a mathematical obstacle to combining approximate gradients with sparsity enforcement and provides an algorithm analyzed around that obstacle.
neurips-2022-zeroth-order-hard-threshold.tldr: SZOHT combines black-box gradient estimates with hard thresholding, with convergence analysis explaining the sampling needed to manage amplified estimation errors.
